passage: At the government school in Kundapur, the boys ate lunch under the big neem tree, and today Lokesh sat at the end of a root with his tiffin unopened. Darshan watched him and felt his own rice turn to paste. Was it yesterday? He'd picked Ganesh first for the kho-kho team, not Lokesh. Or the geometry box he'd returned with a broken compass. By the time the bell rang, Darshan had a whole list and a sore stomach. He finally walked over. 'Lokesh, sorry about the compass. And kho-kho.' Lokesh stared at him. 'What? Oh. No. Our cow's been sick since Sunday. Appa might have to sell her.' He wiped his face. 'I didn't even notice the compass.' Darshan sat down beside him. They shared the tiffin in silence until the second bell.

qa.q: Who did Darshan pick first for the kho-kho team?
qa.a: Darshan picked Ganesh first for the kho-kho team.

qa.q: Why did Darshan's rice 'turn to paste'?
qa.a: Darshan was anxious, sure that Lokesh's silence was about something Darshan had done, so he felt too worried to eat.

qa.q: What choice at the end helped most?
qa.a: Sitting down beside Lokesh and sharing the tiffin, once the real reason was out, turned Darshan's worry into support for a friend having a hard day.

qa.q: What was going on for Lokesh that Darshan couldn't see?
qa.a: Lokesh was worried about the sick cow and Appa perhaps selling her, so the compass and the kho-kho team hadn't even crossed his mind.

grounding: Shows a teenager who sees a friend silent at lunch and assumes it is about his own mistakes, when the friend is worried about a sick cow.

passage: In the canteen of their school in Hamburg, Clara let her soup go cold and answered everything with one word. Kaito kept talking about the weekend, then stopped. His mind ran back through the morning. He had copied her answer in chemistry. He had joked about her new haircut. Maybe she'd seen the photo he posted from the class trip, the one where her eyes were half closed. His chest tightened. After school, walking to the station, he blurted, 'Are you angry with me? Is it the photo?' Clara looked honestly confused. 'What photo? No. My grandmother's moving into a care home this week. My mum cried at breakfast.' Kaito felt his face burn, then soften. 'I'm sorry. Do you want to talk about it, or not?' 'Not yet,' Clara said. 'But walk with me.'

qa.q: Where is Clara's grandmother moving this week?
qa.a: Clara's grandmother is moving into a care home this week.

qa.q: Why did Kaito's chest tighten in the canteen?
qa.a: Kaito was anxious that Clara's quiet was about him, and his mind searched the morning for proof: the copied answer, the haircut joke, the photo.

qa.q: How did Kaito's question after school change things?
qa.a: Asking directly, even clumsily, brought out the real reason, and then asking whether Clara wanted to talk let him offer support instead of more worry.

qa.q: How might Clara have felt when Kaito asked about the photo?
qa.a: Clara was probably confused and a little tired, since her mind was on her grandmother and her mum crying, but she still wanted Kaito's company on the walk.

grounding: Shows a teenager who assumes a friend's quiet lunch is about something he did, until she explains a family change.

passage:
At the residential school in Shillong, lunch in the dining hall was usually loud at their table. Today Sonali just pushed rice around her plate and looked out of the window.

Mehak's stomach tightened. What did I do? She went through the morning. She'd borrowed Sonali's geometry box without asking. She'd laughed at Sonali's wrong answer in chemistry. Last night she'd switched off the dorm light while Sonali was still reading.

By the time the plates were cleared, Mehak had a whole list and no appetite. She didn't even hear the housemaster's announcement about the trip.

At prep, she couldn't concentrate. Finally she whispered, "Sonali, are you angry with me? I'm really sorry about the light and the geometry box."

Sonali looked confused. "What? No. My grandmother's not well and I can't go home till the holidays. I've been thinking about her all day."

Mehak sat back. None of the list had anything to do with it.

qa.q: Why had Sonali been quiet, according to her?
qa.a: Her grandmother's not well and she can't go home till the holidays.

qa.q: Why did Mehak feel so sure she had caused Sonali's mood?
qa.a: Mehak was anxious, and her mind searched only her own actions for an explanation, so every small thing looked like a cause. It didn't occur to her that the mood could be about something else.

qa.q: What could Mehak try the next time a friend seems quiet?
qa.a: Ask a gentle, open question like "Are you okay? You seem quiet today" before building a list of her own faults. It leaves room for the real reason.

qa.q: What might it be like for Sonali to hear an apology about the light when she's worried about her grandmother?
qa.a: Sonali might feel puzzled, and maybe a little lonely that Mehak was thinking about herself. But it also gave Sonali a chance to share what was really on her mind.

grounding: A teenage girl sees her friend quiet at lunch and worries about what she did wrong, only to learn the mood has nothing to do with her.

passage:
Sumit,

You've been really quiet all week at lunch and I've been going crazy thinking about it. So here's a note, because I'm bad at saying things.

If it's because I made fun of your haircut on Monday, I'm sorry. If it's because I sat with Arvind at the assembly, I'm sorry. If it's because I didn't pass you the ball in football, that was an accident. If it's the thing I said about your cycle, I didn't mean it.

I've lost sleep over this. Just tell me what I did and I'll fix it.

Mridul

----

(Sumit's reply, written underneath in pencil:)

Bhai, you idiot, none of that. My dad lost his job two weeks ago and everything at home is weird. It's not you. I just don't feel like talking much.

Walk home together today?

S.

qa.q: Why has Sumit been quiet, according to his reply?
qa.a: Sumit's dad lost his job two weeks ago and everything at home is weird.

qa.q: Why did Mridul list so many things he might have done wrong?
qa.a: Mridul was anxious and assumed Sumit's mood must be about him, so he searched every small moment for a cause. Losing sleep shows how sure he was that it was his fault.

qa.q: What went well in how this was finally cleared up, and what could Mridul do now?
qa.a: Mridul asked directly instead of staying silent, which gave Sumit a chance to explain. Now he could just walk home with Sumit and be there without needing to fix anything.

qa.q: How might Sumit feel reading a list of apologies for things Sumit hadn't even noticed?
qa.a: Sumit might feel a little amused, calling Mridul an idiot fondly, and also touched that Mridul cares. The note gave Sumit an easy way to share what's really going on.

grounding: A teenage boy notices his friend quiet at lunch and writes a list of apologies, learning the mood was about something at home, not him.
